project.topic: What if all Earth's continents joined into one giant landmass?
project.title: What If All the Continents Joined Into One?
project.audience: Curious global general audiences age 13+, no science background
project.core_question: If all of today's land were pushed together into one supercontinent, how would weather, people and wildlife change, and will it really happen again?
project.viewer_takeaway: Continents drift about as fast as fingernails grow and have joined before; one giant landmass would trap a vast desert in its heart, crowd life onto stormy coasts, cost species and reefs, and the next supercontinent may be too hot for most mammals.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Today Earth's land, about 29% of its surface, is split into several continents separated by oceans. The plates carrying them move roughly as fast as fingernails grow. Around 200 million years ago almost all land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, which then split apart; climate models and rocks show it had a megamonsoon and a very dry interior.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: All of today's continents are joined into one compact landmass, arranged like Pangaea, keeping today's land area, Sun and air. The film shows the joining as a sped-up schematic and compares it with the real past (Pangaea) and a modelled future supercontinent (Pangea Ultima).
assumptions: Total land area, ocean volume, the Sun and atmospheric composition stay as they are today; only the arrangement of the continents changes.
The joined arrangement is a Pangaea-like schematic, not an exact reconstruction; continent outlines are today's.
The climate response follows physical principles seen in Pangaea and in models: moisture comes mostly from open water, and land far from the sea has larger temperature swings.

The heat figures in S08 come from a published model of the next supercontinent about 250 million years from now, which also includes a brighter Sun and more CO2; they are not predictions for today's Sun.
causal_chain: Plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow; over hundreds of millions of years continents gather and split.
Joining all land into one compact mass puts its interior thousands of kilometres from the nearest sea.
About 90% of atmospheric moisture evaporates from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers, so rain falls mostly near the coasts and the interior becomes very dry.
Far from the moderating ocean, the interior swings between extremely hot days and frigid nights, while the coasts get strong seasonal monsoons.
People would cluster on the wetter, milder coasts.
Joined land lets species spread everywhere; competition can wipe out many, as when the Americas joined.
One landmass has far less coastline and fewer shallow coastal seas, the habitat of coral reefs.
A future supercontinent, with a brighter Sun and more CO2, could leave only 8–16% of land habitable for mammals in one model.
uncertainties: The exact arrangement and timing of the next supercontinent are uncertain; several configurations have been proposed (Pangea Ultima, Amasia, Novopangaea).
How dry the interior becomes depends on the shape of the landmass, mountains and ocean currents; the dry-interior overlay is schematic.
Species losses after continents join depend on the animals involved; the tabletop diorama is illustrative.
The 8–16% habitability figure is one model result and includes future solar brightening and higher CO2.

claims.statement: Almost all of Earth's land was once joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, which began to split apart about 200 million years ago.
claims.reasoning: USGS This Dynamic Earth: "around 200 million years ago, the supercontinent Pangaea began to split apart".
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "about two hundred million years ago"; label the joined arrangement as schematic.

claims.statement: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together remarkably well, one of the first clues that they were once joined.
claims.reasoning: USGS This Dynamic Earth describes the remarkable fit of the South American and African continents, first noted by Abraham Ortelius.

claims.statement: Tectonic plates move at roughly the rate fingernails grow.
claims.reasoning: USGS FAQ "How fast do tectonic plates move?"
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use the fingernail comparison; no single speed number.

claims.statement: Joining all land (about 29% of Earth's surface, roughly 150 million km²) into one compact mass would put its interior thousands of kilometres from the sea.
claims.reasoning: USGS: about 71% of Earth's surface is water-covered, so land ≈ 0.29 × 510 million km² ≈ 148 million km²; a compact shape of that area has an equivalent radius of roughly 6,900 km, so its centre lies thousands of kilometres from any coast.
claims.presentation_guardrail: On-screen "thousands of km from the sea" only.

claims.statement: Pangaea's climate had a megamonsoon and an immensely arid interior with extremely hot days and frigid nights.
claims.reasoning: Pangean megamonsoon (Wikipedia), citing Kutzbach & Gallimore (1989) and Parrish (1993).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate "would"; desert and monsoon scenes are illustrative.

claims.statement: Coasts have milder temperatures because water's high heat capacity moderates them; inland areas have much wider daily and seasonal temperature ranges.
claims.reasoning: NASA-funded Climate Science Investigations module (Land and water).

claims.statement: On a supercontinent most people would live on the wetter, milder coasts.
claims.reasoning: Rain and moderate temperatures concentrate near coasts (CL05, CL06, CL13); settlement follows water and mild climate.

claims.statement: When North and South America connected, South American mammals went extinct at a disproportionately high rate; almost half of living South American mammals descend from North American immigrants, against about 10% the other way.
claims.reasoning: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute study in PNAS (2020), reported by ScienceDaily.

claims.statement: Joining every continent would let species spread everywhere, and many could be lost to competition.
claims.reasoning: Generalised from the Great American Biotic Interchange (CL08).

claims.statement: One merged landmass has far less coastline than several separate continents, so there would be fewer shallow coastal seas.
claims.reasoning: Coastlines disappear where continents meet, and a single compact shape has a much smaller perimeter for the same area.

claims.statement: Most reef-building corals live in shallow tropical and subtropical waters, mostly where light reaches to about 30 metres.

A University of Bristol–led model of the next supercontinent, Pangea Ultima (expected within about 250 million years), finds widespread 40–50 °C temperatures and only 8–16% of land habitable for mammals, due to continentality, a brighter Sun and more CO2.
claims.reasoning: University of Bristol press release on the Nature Geoscience paper "Climate extremes likely to drive land mammal extinction during next supercontinent assembly" (2023).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Label "model result"; the globe shape is schematic.

claims.statement: About 90% of the moisture in the atmosphere evaporates from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.
claims.reasoning: USGS Water Science School, Evaporation and the Water Cycle.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate "most moisture rises from the sea".

creative_direction.logline: Today's continents slide together into one giant landmass, and we follow the consequences from orbit to a dry heart, stormy coasts, a meeting of animals and a coral sea, to a hotter future, before the map eases back to today.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Premium documentary realism with a geological palette: deep ocean blues, NASA-true continents, rust-red desert and storm greys; schematics are clean tabletop or orbital overlays in warm orange and pale blue.
creative_direction.lighting: Hard space sunlight for orbital shots; harsh white sun inland; dim storm light on the coast; soft studio light for the diorama; sun shafts underwater.
creative_direction.camera_language: Slow orbits and push-ins from space, close views of the South Atlantic seam, low glides over dunes and coasts, eye-level human scale, a tabletop diorama and an underwater glide.
creative_direction.motion_language: Unhurried, inevitable motion: continents grind together, rain sweeps, the needle climbs; nothing jumps.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Orbital shots use 1 unit = 1 Earth radius with true continent outlines (motion sped up, arrangement schematic). Ground scenes use metres at true scale (dunes ~15 m, trees 6–9 m, person 1.75 m, corals 0.3–1.2 m). The diorama is a labelled schematic.
creative_direction.opening_hook: Today's Earth from space: the continents start sliding together while the question is asked.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: The supercontinent eases back apart into today's map, matching the opening frame.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The last frame is today's Earth exactly as at frame 0, just before the continents begin to move.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the studio library first (Earth textures, starfield, cloud shell, dunes, sky, ocean, rain, cloud base, trees, grass, humanoid, dial gauge, underwater volume, fish school, captions, labels, camera rig, pipeline, audio kit, thumbnail composer). New plate-drift globe and coral mounds are original procedural work promoted to the library.

audio.voice_style: Calm, peaceful, warm adult male; intimate documentary voice; natural breathing; wonder without shouting
audio.music_direction: Original slow pad in C minor with deep, grinding low textures for moving continents; open fifths for the supercontinent reveal; a warmer major lift underwater; a tense low swell for the hot future; resolving to C major on the return to today.
audio.sfx_direction: Synthesized and restrained: low tectonic rumble, a soft click as coasts meet, ocean and desert wind, monsoon rain with distant thunder, footsteps of many small animals, muffled underwater ambience, dry heat crackle.

captions.style: Premium documentary subtitles: ivory semibold with a thin charcoal outline and soft shadow, restrained amber active word, phrase-by-phrase with a 120 ms ease; a soft dark band behind text over bright scenes.
captions.active_word_treatment: The spoken word turns amber without moving the baseline; emphasised phrases keep a soft accent, a 1.04 scale or a gentle glow.
captions.highlights_policy: Exact narration only. In-scene labels are limited to chips, schematic/illustrative/model tags and numbers backed by the claim register.

distribution.primary_search_intent: what if all continents joined together
distribution.distinctive_angle: Push today's continents together and Earth gains a desert heart, monsoon-battered coasts, fewer species and reefs, and the real next supercontinent may be too hot for most mammals.
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Pangaea and plate speed are established (USGS); the joined arrangement and climate scenes are schematic or illustrative; the 8–16% habitability figure is one published model of the next supercontinent. Titles must not claim it will happen soon.
